note: Source record for the 50-plant reverse-build batch supplied by Oscar on 2026-08-10. The card schema in timber.html has no home for foliage, container, hardinessNote, toxicity or the source's declared-uncertain list, so they are kept here rather than dropped. Toxicity is folded into each card's `resilience` (the Lonicera/Gunnera precedent) and compliance into `type` + `returnRisk`. Keyed by the `latin` value used on the card. 1 of the 50 was dealt (Chamaerops humilis, photo already on disk); the other 49 are in PLANTS_ON_HOLD awaiting photographs.

Tetrapanax papyrifer 'Rex'.hardinessNote: Suitable for mild and sheltered UK gardens. Frost commonly removes the foliage and may kill stems back to ground level, but an established mulched root system can reshoot in spring.
Tetrapanax papyrifer 'Rex'.toxicity: Fine hairs on young growth may irritate skin, eyes or airways in sensitive people; gloves are sensible when handling or cutting.
uncertain: Final size and winter behaviour vary greatly with climate; plants may behave as large woody shrubs in mild sites or die back almost to ground level after colder winters.
Underground suckering can extend beyond the nominal canopy spread, so the displayed spread is not a containment limit.

Dicksonia antarctica.hardinessNote: The crown is vulnerable below roughly -5°C. In much of the UK the crown should be packed with dry straw, fleece or similar insulation before significant frost, with extra protection around the upper trunk in colder areas.
Dicksonia antarctica.compliance: Commercially harvested Australian tree ferns may be subject to source-country harvesting, tagging and trade controls. Source stated Dicksonia antarctica is not currently listed under CITES for trade restrictions — NOT VERIFIED, see VERIFY-QUEUE item 16.
uncertain: Trunk growth is exceptionally slow, commonly around 2.5cm per year under UK garden conditions, so purchased trunk height largely determines the plant's apparent size for many years.
Fronds may be lost in colder winters even when the protected crown survives.

Rhus typhina.hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK, tolerating severe winter cold once established.
Rhus typhina.toxicity: Sap may irritate sensitive skin. Wear gloves when pruning or handling cut stems.
uncertain: Plants are dioecious, so the conspicuous crimson fruiting heads are normally produced only by female plants after pollination.
Root suckers can extend beyond the nominal mature canopy spread.

Rodgersia 'Bronze Peacock'.hardinessNote: Fully hardy through the UK once established; foliage dies down in winter while the crown remains dormant below ground.
uncertain: The current RHS accepted name is Rodgersia 'Bronze Peacock', rather than Rodgersia podophylla 'Bronze Peacock'.
The supplied shopping-list description gave cream flowers, but the cultivar is described by RHS as producing bright pink flowers.

Rhododendron 'Homebush'.hardinessNote: Very hardy in UK gardens, although an exposed position can damage flowers or developing buds.
Rhododendron 'Homebush'.toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten and can be toxic to people, pets and livestock.
uncertain: Ultimate dimensions vary with soil, climate and pruning; mature plants may gradually exceed typical garden-centre label dimensions.

Rhododendron luteum.hardinessNote: Very hardy through the UK once established.
Rhododendron luteum.toxicity: All parts are poisonous if eaten and are potentially dangerous to people, pets and livestock.
Rhododendron luteum.compliance: Listed in Schedule 9 Part II of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 in England and Wales. Do not plant or otherwise cause this species to grow in the wild, and prevent garden material from escaping into natural habitats.
uncertain: Legal restrictions vary between UK jurisdictions; this compliance note specifically reflects its Schedule 9 status in England and Wales.

Trachycarpus fortunei.hardinessNote: One of the most reliably hardy palms for UK gardens and capable of tolerating around -15°C or below in a sheltered position once established.
uncertain: Garden specimens are often sold and labelled at much smaller projected sizes, but old plants can eventually exceed 12m.

Chamaerops humilis.hardinessNote: Hardier than its Mediterranean appearance suggests but less cold tolerant than Trachycarpus fortunei; severe UK winters can damage leaves or stems.
Chamaerops humilis.toxicity: Leaf stalks can carry sharp spines capable of causing physical injury; site away from narrow paths and children's play areas.

Melianthus major.hardinessNote: Top growth is vulnerable in cold UK winters. Established crowns often reshoot after moderate frost in sheltered gardens but require protection in colder areas.
Melianthus major.toxicity: Do not eat. Melianthus contains potentially toxic compounds and should be treated as an ornamental plant rather than an edible one.
uncertain: Foliage is often described as having a peanut-butter-like scent when bruised, but scent perception is subjective.
It may remain evergreen in frost-free conditions or behave almost herbaceously after colder winters.

Astelia chathamica.hardinessNote: Best suited to mild or sheltered UK gardens. Severe frost and cold drying winds can damage or kill exposed foliage.
uncertain: 'Silver Spear' is commonly encountered in trade, but RHS treats 'Silver Spear' as a synonym associated with Astelia chathamica rather than as the accepted cultivar name, so the accepted species name is used here.

Fargesia rufa.hardinessNote: Hardy across most UK gardens and substantially more cold tolerant than many ornamental bamboos.
uncertain: Fargesia rufa is commonly sold informally as an umbrella bamboo, but RHS uses dragon head bamboo; true umbrella bamboo is more commonly applied to Fargesia murielae.

Phyllostachys nigra.hardinessNote: Hardy through most UK gardens once established.
uncertain: New canes are green and generally develop their characteristic dark colour with age, so young nursery plants may have few genuinely black culms.
Rhizome spread can substantially exceed the displayed canopy width.

Arbutus unedo.hardinessNote: Hardy in many UK gardens, particularly in mild, sheltered and coastal areas; young growth can be damaged by severe frost.
Arbutus unedo.toxicity: Ripe fruits are edible but are generally valued more as an ornamental feature than as a high-quality dessert fruit.

Tamarix ramosissima 'Pink Cascade'.hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK, though young growth benefits from some protection from very cold drying winds inland.

Pieris 'Forest Flame'.hardinessNote: Hardy across most of the UK, although young plants and fresh spring growth can be damaged in exposed frosty positions.
Pieris 'Forest Flame'.toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten and potentially toxic to people and animals.
uncertain: The current RHS accepted name is Pieris 'Forest Flame'; it is often sold in the trade as Pieris japonica 'Forest Flame'.

Skimmia japonica 'Rubella'.hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most of the UK in a sheltered garden position.
Skimmia japonica 'Rubella'.toxicity: Ornamental plant; do not eat any plant material.
uncertain: 'Rubella' is a male cultivar and therefore does not itself produce the conspicuous berry crop associated with female skimmias.

Ceanothus 'Concha'.hardinessNote: Hardy in many UK gardens but vulnerable to severe frost, cold winds and wet winters; a warm sheltered site markedly improves reliability.
uncertain: Individual lifespan varies considerably with site and climate; 'short-lived' is a useful horticultural caution rather than a fixed lifespan.

Physocarpus opulifolius 'Diabolo'.hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy and suitable for even very cold UK gardens.

Sambucus nigra f. porphyrophylla 'Eva'.toxicity: Leaves, stems and unripe fruit contain potentially harmful cyanogenic compounds. Flowers and properly prepared ripe berries are the traditionally used edible parts.
uncertain: Black Lace is the trade designation; 'Eva' is the cultivar denomination used in the accepted botanical name.
Hard coppicing improves foliage effect but reduces or delays flowering compared with lightly pruned plants.

Daphne bholua 'Jacqueline Postill'.hardinessNote: Generally hardy in sheltered UK gardens but flower buds and evergreen foliage can be damaged by severe cold or exposure.
Daphne bholua 'Jacqueline Postill'.toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten, with the berries particularly dangerous. Sap may also irritate skin.
uncertain: Foliage retention varies with winter severity; colder sites may see greater leaf loss.

Sarcococca confusa.hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most of the UK.
Sarcococca confusa.toxicity: Berries are ornamental and should not be treated as edible.

Chaenomeles × superba 'Crimson and Gold'.toxicity: The hard aromatic fruit is commonly cooked for preserves; avoid eating the seeds.

Aucuba japonica 'Crotonifolia'.toxicity: Berries are ornamental and should not be eaten.
uncertain: 'Crotonifolia' is female, but a nearby male pollinator is normally required for reliable berry production.

Kalmia latifolia 'Ostbo Red'.hardinessNote: Hardy in most UK gardens provided roots are healthy and the plant is not exposed to severe drying winds.
Kalmia latifolia 'Ostbo Red'.toxicity: All parts are highly poisonous if eaten and can be dangerous to people, pets and livestock.
uncertain: Cultivar size is strongly influenced by age and site because Kalmia develops slowly and old plants may become substantially larger than typical nursery specimens.

Enkianthus campanulatus.hardinessNote: Very hardy in suitable soil throughout the UK.

Fothergilla major.hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most of the UK.

Betula utilis subsp. jacquemontii 'Doore.hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy and suitable throughout the UK.
uncertain: The accepted RHS name uses subsp. jacquemontii rather than var. jacquemontii.
The bark becomes progressively whiter with maturity; young nursery plants may not yet show the full mature effect.

Amelanchier lamarckii.toxicity: Ripe berries are edible and are also readily taken by birds.

Nyssa sylvatica 'Wisley Bonfire'.hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK once established, provided soil and moisture requirements are met.
uncertain: 'Wisley Bonfire' is a male selection, so ornamental fruit is not expected.

Corylus avellana 'Contorta'.toxicity: Nuts, when produced and fully mature, are edible.
uncertain: Not every plant encountered in cultivation is necessarily on the same rootstock, so the sucker warning applies specifically to grafted specimens.

Malus 'Evereste'.toxicity: Crab apples can be cooked for jelly and preserves. As with other apples, avoid eating substantial quantities of crushed seeds.
uncertain: 'Evereste' has a long flowering period and is a useful pollination partner for many apples, but calling any single crab apple a literally universal pollinator overstates compatibility.

Koelreuteria paniculata.hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK but performs best with summer heat and shelter.

uncertain: 'Sunburst' belongs to the thornless form, f. inermis, and should not develop the formidable trunk thorns associated with typical Gleditsia triacanthos.

Eucalyptus gunnii Azura ('Cagire').hardinessNote: Selected for improved hardiness and compact growth; established plants are hardy through most UK gardens, though young shoots can be damaged by severe frost.
Eucalyptus gunnii Azura ('Cagire').toxicity: Eucalyptus foliage and concentrated eucalyptus oils are harmful if ingested in quantity and should be kept away from pets and children.
uncertain: Azura is the trade designation and 'Cagire' is the cultivar denomination.
Ultimate size depends enormously on whether the plant is regularly coppiced or allowed to form a tree.

Wisteria floribunda f. multijuga.hardinessNote: Very hardy once established, though spring flowers can be damaged by late frost.
Wisteria floribunda f. multijuga.toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten, with the seeds and pods particularly poisonous.
uncertain: The accepted botanical name is Wisteria floribunda f. multijuga rather than the cultivar-style Wisteria floribunda 'Multijuga'.
Grafted named plants generally flower substantially sooner and more predictably than seed-raised wisterias.

Trachelospermum jasminoides.hardinessNote: Hardy in many sheltered UK gardens but vulnerable to severe frost and cold drying winds, particularly when young.
Trachelospermum jasminoides.toxicity: Milky sap can irritate skin and the plant should not be eaten.

Hedera colchica 'Sulphur Heart'.toxicity: Harmful if eaten and sap may cause skin irritation or allergic dermatitis. Also potentially harmful to pets.

Akebia quinata.hardinessNote: Very hardy in UK gardens, although foliage may be more deciduous in colder conditions.
Akebia quinata.toxicity: The soft pulp of fully ripe fruit is edible, though the plant is primarily ornamental and the seeds are not normally eaten.
uncertain: Reliable fruiting generally requires cross-pollination from a genetically different compatible plant, so simply planting two clonally identical specimens may not be sufficient.
Rozanne is the trade designation and 'Gerwat' is the cultivar denomination.
The plant is sterile, which contributes to its exceptionally long flowering period because energy is not diverted into a normal seed crop.

Erysimum 'Bowles’s Mauve'.hardinessNote: Generally hardy in well-drained UK gardens but severe cold and winter wet can shorten its life.
Erysimum 'Bowles’s Mauve'.toxicity: Potentially harmful if eaten; grow as an ornamental rather than an edible plant.
uncertain: The often-quoted two- to three-year lifespan is not absolute; lifespan varies considerably with drainage, winter weather and pruning.
Despite the name 'Walker's Low', the cultivar is not especially tiny and can approach around 60-90cm in favourable rich ground.

Helleborus (Rodney Davey Marbled Group).toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten and sap may irritate skin; wear gloves when cutting foliage.
uncertain: Anna's Red is the trade name associated with cultivar denomination 'Abcrd02' and belongs to the Rodney Davey Marbled Group/Frostkiss breeding series.
Blanket removal of every leaf in January is unnecessary for this strongly marbled evergreen selection; remove old or diseased foliage selectively.

Hakonechloa macra 'Aureola'.hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy while dormant and suitable throughout the UK.
uncertain: Spring emergence can be several weeks later than many neighbouring perennials, particularly after cold winters.
